🎓 Habit & Systems Literature

The thinking HSG is built on — well-known authors, their core teachings, and the books they come from.

Well-Known Authors & Thinkers

⚙️
James Clear
Systems over goals
Clear's central argument is that goals set a direction but systems are what actually produce results — winners and losers in any field often share the same goal, so the goal itself can't be what separates them. He frames habits as identity statements in disguise: every time you complete a small action, you're casting a vote for the type of person you wish to become, and enough votes eventually change your self-image. He also breaks every habit down into a four-part loop — cue, craving, response, reward — and argues you change a habit by redesigning that loop with what he calls the Four Laws: make it obvious, make it attractive, make it easy, and make it satisfying (or reverse each law to break a bad one).
📚
Jim Rohn
Daily personal disciplines
Rohn spent decades arguing that the gap between where you are and where you want to be is almost never a single decision — it's the slow accumulation of small, ordinary choices repeated (or skipped) day after day. He called this idea "the slight edge": a good habit and a bad habit can look almost identical in the moment, costing or gaining you almost nothing on any single day, but the two paths diverge dramatically once time is allowed to compound. His practical takeaway was to treat personal development — reading, reflection, goal review, and self-discipline — as a daily job in its own right, not an occasional event you get to when you feel like it.
🧩
Stephen Covey
Principle-centered effectiveness
Covey's framework rests on the idea that durable effectiveness comes from aligning your actions with timeless principles — fairness, integrity, honesty, service — rather than chasing techniques or quick fixes. His habits move a person from dependence to independence ("Be Proactive," "Begin with the End in Mind," "Put First Things First") and then from independence to interdependence ("Think Win-Win," "Seek First to Understand, Then to Be Understood," "Synergize"), capped by a seventh habit, "Sharpen the Saw," about ongoing renewal across physical, mental, social, and spiritual dimensions. His time-management matrix — sorting tasks by urgent vs. important — is one of the most widely borrowed ideas in productivity writing, including HSG's own Eisenhower Matrix planning tool.
🧠
Charles Duhigg
Psychology of habit loops
Duhigg's reporting-driven case for how habits work centers on a neurological loop: a cue triggers a routine, which delivers a reward, and with enough repetition the brain starts craving the reward as soon as it senses the cue — at which point the behavior becomes close to automatic. His most practical claim is that habits are rarely deleted outright; instead, lasting change usually comes from keeping the same cue and the same reward while consciously swapping out the routine in between. He also popularized the idea of "keystone habits" — a small number of habits (like regular exercise or making your bed) that, once established, tend to trigger a cascade of unrelated positive changes elsewhere in a person's life.
🔬
BJ Fogg
Micro-behavior design
Fogg, a Stanford behavior scientist, argues that motivation is an unreliable foundation to build habits on because it naturally rises and falls. His alternative is to design behaviors so tiny they require almost no motivation at all — his own shorthand recipe is "After I [existing routine], I will [new tiny behavior]" — and then to deliberately feel a moment of genuine positive emotion immediately afterward. In his model, it's that felt emotion, not repetition by itself, that wires a new habit into the brain, which is why he insists on celebrating even the smallest win. He summarizes the conditions for any behavior to occur with the formula B = MAP: Behavior happens when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt all converge at the same moment.
📈
Darren Hardy
Compounding daily choices
Hardy, the former publisher of SUCCESS magazine, built his case around what he calls the compound effect: small, seemingly insignificant choices — an extra ten minutes of reading, one fewer unnecessary purchase, one uncomfortable phone call made instead of avoided — produce dramatically outsized results when repeated consistently over months and years, in either direction. Because the effects are invisible day-to-day, he argues that tracking your choices and staying patient through the boring middle stretch matters more than any burst of short-term intensity. His practical tool, sometimes called the "Big 3," is to identify the small number of daily choices that matter most to a goal and simply track whether you did them, every single day.
💡
Napoleon Hill
Definite life aims
Hill's work, built from years of interviews with the highly successful people of his era, centers on the idea of a "definite major purpose" — a single, clearly written aim pursued with persistence and organized daily effort — as the force that channels energy that would otherwise scatter across too many half-finished intentions. He paired that definiteness of purpose with what he called "applied faith": a burning desire, a concrete plan, and consistent action taken whether or not motivation happens to be present that day. His enduring influence on later habit and success writers is largely in this insistence that clarity of aim, written down and revisited daily, is what turns a vague wish into a pursued goal.

Well-Known Books

📕
Atomic Habits
by James Clear
Lays out the case for systems over goals and introduces the four-part habit loop (cue, craving, response, reward) alongside the Four Laws of Behavior Change — make it obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying — as the practical levers for building good habits and breaking bad ones. It also popularized "habit stacking" (the formula this page's Habit Stacker tool is built around) and identity-based habits, the idea that lasting change starts with deciding who you want to become rather than what you want to achieve.
🌱
The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
by Stephen R. Covey
Organizes effectiveness around seven habits that move a person from dependence to independence and then to interdependence — proactivity, beginning with the end in mind, prioritizing what's important over what's merely urgent, thinking win-win, seeking to understand before being understood, synergizing with others, and renewing yourself continually. It argues these habits work because they're rooted in stable principles rather than trends, which is why the framework has stayed in wide use for decades.
🔄
The Power of Habit
by Charles Duhigg
Uses case studies from individuals, companies, and social movements to explain the cue-routine-reward loop and how habits form, persist, and can be deliberately redirected by changing the routine while keeping the same cue and reward. It extends the idea beyond individuals to organizations and even societies, showing how a small number of "keystone habits" can trigger wide-reaching change well beyond the original behavior.
🌱
Tiny Habits
by BJ Fogg
Presents Fogg's Behavior Design method for making change easy rather than relying on willpower: shrink the new behavior down until it's almost trivially small, anchor it immediately after an existing routine, and celebrate right away to create a genuine positive feeling. The book's B=MAP formula (Behavior = Motivation + Ability + Prompt) offers a simple diagnostic for why a habit isn't sticking — usually because the behavior is too big for the motivation available, not because the person lacks willpower.
📈
The Compound Effect
by Darren Hardy
Makes the case that success is rarely the result of luck or big breaks, but of small, ordinary decisions compounded consistently over a long enough time horizon. It offers practical tools for applying the idea — tracking your "Big 3" daily choices, auditing your current habits and influences, and understanding momentum — so the compounding effect works in your favor instead of quietly working against you.
💡
Think and Grow Rich
by Napoleon Hill
Distills patterns Hill observed across interviews with many of the most successful people of his time into principles built around definiteness of purpose, persistence, and organized daily planning. Its central claim is that a clearly defined, burning desire — paired with a concrete plan and consistent, faith-backed action — is what separates people who achieve extraordinary goals from those who only ever intend to.

💡 Two Ideas Worth Building Your Systems Around

On starting small — Atomic Habits
The Two-Minute Rule
Almost any habit can be scaled down to something that takes less than two minutes: "read one page," not "read for an hour," "put on running shoes," not "run 5k." The point isn't that two minutes is enough — it's that showing up is the habit you're actually practicing. Once you're the type of person who shows up, scaling up is the easy part. Use the "starter version" field below to force yourself to define this for every system.
On sticking with it — Jim Rohn
Discipline Outlasts Motivation
Jim Rohn spent decades teaching that motivation is what gets you to start something, but it's discipline — showing up on the days you don't feel like it — that actually finishes it. Motivation is a mood, and moods pass. A system doesn't need you to feel inspired; it needs you to check the box anyway. That's also why "never miss twice" matters more than "never miss."

🌱 A Few Simple Disciplines, Repeated Daily

Jim Rohn's central argument across his talks and books was disarmingly simple: the difference between where you are and where you want to be usually isn't a lack of information or a single big decision — it's the accumulated weight of small, ordinary choices, repeated (or not) day after day. He liked to point out that the disciplines that matter most are rarely difficult in themselves; skipping them once doesn't cost much either. The cost only shows up much later, once a pattern has had months or years to compound — in either direction. His practical answer was to treat personal development as a daily discipline in its own right, not an occasional event: read something worthwhile most days, reflect on the day's decisions, keep your goals in view, and take deliberate care of your habits the same way you'd take care of a business or a garden.

Discipline 1
Work on yourself first
Rohn's often-repeated advice was to spend at least as much effort developing yourself as you spend on any goal or job. Skills, character, and habits compound across every area of life — a goal is temporary, but who you become from pursuing it stays with you.
Discipline 2
Choose your environment on purpose
Rohn argued that people tend to drift toward the habits and attitudes of whoever and whatever surrounds them — the people, the media, the physical space. If a system keeps failing, check what it's competing against before blaming willpower.
Discipline 3
Track it, don't just intend it
Rohn was a lifelong advocate of keeping a journal and reviewing it — the act of writing something down and checking on it is what turns a vague intention into something you're actually accountable to. The daily dots below exist for exactly this reason.
Discipline 4
Respect the seasons
Rohn often used the metaphor of seasons: you don't get to choose when a hard stretch arrives, but you do get to choose your response to it. A system that only survives when life is easy isn't really a system yet — the aim is a version small enough to survive winter too.
⚡ Putting both ideas to work together: define the two-minute starter version so the system is easy enough to survive a bad day (Atomic Habits), and show up on that minimum version specifically because you don't feel like it (Jim Rohn) — that combination is what actually builds a streak that survives real life.

🎓 Building Systems Education

Frameworks for turning an intention into a routine that runs itself.

🎓 Building Systems — Education

The same 50 authors and books behind the Goals education library, read here through a systems lens — how each one designs the daily machinery that produces results: cues and friction, cadence and review, environment design, execution disciplines and feedback loops. Each framework has a 5 Ws blueprint, the psychology behind it, and exactly how to run it.

1James Clear: The Four-Law Habit System

From Atomic Habits

A goal is a result you want; a system is the set of daily behaviours that produce it. Clear's four laws are the control panel for that system: make the behaviour obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying, and invert all four for anything you want to stop.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, designing the environment rather than relying on willpower.
  • What: A four-lever system applied to every recurring behaviour in your day.
  • Where: In the physical space where the behaviour happens — kitchen, desk, gym bag by the door.
  • When: At the moment of design, not the moment of temptation.
  • Why: Systems survive bad days; motivation doesn't.
Why it works
  • Automaticity rises with repetition, not with intensity — frequency beats effort.
  • Environment is the invisible hand: cue salience predicts behaviour better than intention.
  • Each rep is a vote for an identity; the identity then defends the system.
How to run it

1Audit the cue layer

Walk your home and workplace and list every cue that currently triggers an unwanted behaviour. Remove or hide each one, then add a visible cue for the replacement.

2Shrink the response

Scale the new behaviour down until it takes two minutes. Master showing up before you optimise the workout.

3Close the loop

Attach an immediate, visible reward — a tick in the tracker in this app counts. Never miss twice.

2Michael Hyatt: The Weekly Review Operating Rhythm

From Free to Focus / Your Best Year Ever

Hyatt's systems contribution is cadence: an annual plan is worthless without a weekly ritual that pulls it back into contact with reality. The Ideal Week, the Weekly Preview and the Daily Big 3 form a nested loop.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, in the role of manager of yourself rather than worker.
  • What: A recurring review meeting with one attendee, held on the calendar like any other commitment.
  • Where: Somewhere away from your normal work surface, so the mode shift is physical.
  • When: Same 60-minute slot every week — protected first, everything else after.
  • Why: Without review, systems drift silently for months.
Why it works
  • Regular review converts vague intention into scheduled behaviour.
  • Scoring last week creates feedback; feedback is what makes a system self-correcting.
  • Three daily priorities fit working memory; ten do not.
How to run it

1Draft an Ideal Week

Block the template week you'd run if nothing interfered: focus, meetings, recovery, family. It's a budget, not a prediction.

2Run the Weekly Preview

Review wins, review the calendar ahead, then choose next week's three outcomes.

3Choose a Daily Big 3

Each morning, name three tasks that would make the day a success and do them before anything reactive.

3Brian Tracy: Eat That Frog Sequencing

From Eat That Frog!

Tracy's system is a prioritisation algorithm: single-handle the hardest, highest-leverage task first, before decision energy is spent on trivia.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, at the start of the working day.
  • What: The ABCDE method: rank tasks by consequence, not urgency, then execute A1 alone.
  • Where: At your primary work surface, notifications off.
  • When: In the first 90 minutes, before the inbox opens.
  • Why: Consequence-ranked work compounds; urgency-ranked work merely finishes.
Why it works
  • Decision fatigue makes late-day prioritisation unreliable — front-load the hard call.
  • Single-handling avoids the 20–40% switch cost of task interleaving.
  • Completing a high-consequence task early creates momentum for the rest of the day.
How to run it

1List and letter

Write tomorrow's tasks tonight and letter them A–E by consequence, never by how they feel.

2Eat the frog

Start on A1 first thing and stay on it until it's done.

3Protect the block

Treat the first block as unbookable; move meetings into the afternoon.

4Napoleon Hill: Definite Chief Aim + Mastermind Loop

From Think and Grow Rich

Hill's system pairs a written definite aim with daily autosuggestion and a mastermind group — a feedback structure that keeps the aim alive when enthusiasm fades.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You plus a small circle of committed peers.
  • What: A written aim read aloud twice daily and reviewed with the group.
  • Where: Anywhere private for the reading; a fixed venue or call for the group.
  • When: Morning and night for the reading; weekly or fortnightly for the mastermind.
  • Why: Belief is maintained socially, not privately.
Why it works
  • Repeated self-statement shifts what the brain treats as expected and normal.
  • Public commitment raises follow-through through consistency pressure.
  • A peer group supplies correction you cannot generate alone.
How to run it

1Write the aim

One paragraph: what, by when, what you'll give in return, and the plan.

2Read it twice daily

Aloud, with feeling, morning and night — this is the autosuggestion loop.

3Convene the mastermind

Two to six people, fixed agenda, one commitment each per session.

5Caroline Adams Miller: Grit-Backed Goal Systems

From Getting Grit / Creating Your Best Life

Miller's contribution is that systems need difficulty calibrated correctly: hard-but-achievable goals produce more effort than easy ones, provided support scaffolding exists.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, plus at least one person who will notice if you stop.
  • What: Difficulty-calibrated goals supported by deliberate practice and accountability.
  • Where: Wherever the practice happens; the accountability can be remote.
  • When: Set difficulty at planning time; review it monthly as capability grows.
  • Why: Under-ambitious systems decay from boredom; over-ambitious ones from despair.
Why it works
  • Specific hard goals outperform 'do your best' instructions in decades of research.
  • Grit is passion plus perseverance sustained across years, not weeks.
  • Deliberate practice requires immediate, specific feedback to work at all.
How to run it

1Calibrate the stretch

Set the target at roughly 70% expected success — hard enough to demand a plan.

2Add deliberate practice

Isolate the weakest sub-skill and rehearse only that, with feedback, twice a week.

3Recruit a witness

Send a weekly one-line progress note to someone whose opinion you value.

6S.J. Scott: Habit Stacking

From Habit Stacking

Scott's system chains many tiny behaviours into one routine block so that a single trigger fires a whole sequence — cheap to maintain because there is only one decision.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, consolidating scattered small tasks.
  • What: A stack of five-minute-or-less behaviours attached to one reliable anchor.
  • Where: The same location every time — the stack borrows the anchor's context.
  • When: Immediately after the anchor habit, no gap.
  • Why: One trigger costs one unit of willpower regardless of stack length.
Why it works
  • Chaining exploits existing automaticity instead of building new triggers.
  • Small units avoid the activation barrier that stops larger routines.
  • A checklist reduces the working-memory cost of the sequence to near zero.
How to run it

1Pick a rock-solid anchor

Something you already do daily without fail, at a fixed time and place.

2Keep every link tiny

Nothing over five minutes; the whole stack should feel trivially doable.

3Use a written checklist

Run the same order every time until the order itself is automatic.

7Mark Murphy: HARD Goals as System Inputs

From HARD Goals

Murphy argues SMART goals often produce compliance, not drive. HARD — Heartfelt, Animated, Required, Difficult — supplies the emotional fuel a system needs to survive months of unglamorous repetition.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, choosing which goals deserve a system at all.
  • What: An emotional and visual qualification test applied before any planning.
  • Where: In your planning document, before the first task is written.
  • When: At goal-selection time and again whenever motivation dips.
  • Why: Systems built on goals you don't care about are abandoned quietly.
Why it works
  • Vivid mental imagery increases goal commitment and recall.
  • Perceived necessity ('required') beats desirability for follow-through.
  • Difficulty engages attention; easy targets are ignored by the brain's priority system.
How to run it

1Test heartfelt

Write three reasons the goal matters to you personally, not to anyone else.

2Animate it

Describe in the present tense what the day looks like once it's true.

3Make it required

Name the cost of not doing it, and put a date on that cost.

8Hal Elrod: The Morning Routine Stack (S.A.V.E.R.S.)

From The Miracle Morning

Elrod's system front-loads six practices into a fixed morning block so that the day's most important inputs happen before the world intervenes.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, before anyone else needs you.
  • What: Six inputs — silence, affirmations, visualisation, exercise, reading, scribing — in one block.
  • Where: A fixed spot away from the bedroom and away from the phone.
  • When: First 30–60 minutes after waking, same time daily.
  • Why: Whatever you do first tends to be the only thing that survives a chaotic day.
Why it works
  • Morning cortisol peak makes the first hour biologically suited to demanding inputs.
  • A fixed sequence eliminates decision-making while still half-asleep.
  • Early wins create behavioural momentum that carries into unrelated tasks.
How to run it

1Shrink to six minutes

Run one minute of each element for the first fortnight to establish the slot.

2Prepare the night before

Clothes, book, water and journal laid out; alarm across the room.

3Protect the block

No screens until the block is finished — the phone is the routine's main predator.

9Gary Keller: The ONE Thing Focusing Question

From The ONE Thing

Keller's system is subtractive: rather than adding routines, it repeatedly asks what single activity makes everything else easier or unnecessary, then time-blocks it.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, when the list has grown faster than the day.
  • What: A four-hour daily block reserved for the highest-leverage activity.
  • Where: A location where you can be unreachable.
  • When: Early and daily — Keller's rule is to block it before anything else can claim the time.
  • Why: Extraordinary results come from disproportionate time on one thing.
Why it works
  • Attention is a zero-sum resource; parallel priorities produce serial mediocrity.
  • Long uninterrupted blocks are required for work with high cognitive set-up cost.
  • Cascading the question links today's block to a multi-year outcome.
How to run it

1Ask the question

'What's the ONE thing I can do such that by doing it everything else is easier or unnecessary?'

2Block four hours

Recurring, in the calendar, defended like surgery.

3Build a bunker

Physical and digital barriers so the block is genuinely uninterrupted.

10Stephen Covey: Quadrant II Scheduling

From The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People

Covey's system routes time to Quadrant II — important but not urgent — by scheduling priorities rather than prioritising the schedule.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, in each of your defined life roles.
  • What: A weekly plan built from roles and Quadrant II priorities before the calendar fills.
  • Where: In your weekly planning session.
  • When: Weekly, ahead of the week — not daily triage.
  • Why: Urgency-driven systems always crowd out prevention, planning and relationships.
Why it works
  • Prevention work has delayed payoff, so it loses every fair fight against urgency.
  • Role-based planning prevents one domain from silently consuming the others.
  • Scheduling big rocks first is the only reliable way they fit.
How to run it

1List your roles

Six or fewer: e.g. parent, professional, friend, self.

2Set one Q-II goal per role

Important, not urgent, and doable this week.

3Place the big rocks

Put those blocks in the calendar before anything else is allowed in.

11Jon Acuff: The Day-After-Perfect Recovery Rule

From Finish

Acuff's system targets the real failure point: not day one, but the day after you break the streak. Building a planned recovery path into the system makes perfectionism survivable.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, on the day after a failure.
  • What: A pre-written rule that defines the smallest acceptable version of the habit.
  • Where: Written into the habit's definition, not decided in the moment.
  • When: Before you ever miss — the rule must exist in advance.
  • Why: Perfectionism kills more systems than laziness does.
Why it works
  • Abstinence-violation effect: one lapse triggers abandonment unless reframed in advance.
  • Halving the goal mid-stream raises completion rates rather than lowering them.
  • Self-compassion after failure predicts faster resumption than self-criticism.
How to run it

1Write the minimum

Define the 'bad day' version now: one push-up, one paragraph, one call.

2Cut the goal in half

When you're behind, halve the target instead of quitting.

3Never miss twice

Make resumption the rule; the streak is secondary.

12John Lee Dumas: The 100-Day Focus Cycle

From The Common Path to Uncommon Success

Dumas runs goals in short cycles with a single output metric and a public commitment, so the system produces visible evidence long before the goal is reached.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, working in fixed-length seasons rather than open-ended effort.
  • What: One goal, one metric, one hundred days, reviewed publicly.
  • Where: In your tracker and on whatever channel your audience or accountability partner uses.
  • When: Start of each quarter; review weekly inside the cycle.
  • Why: Open-ended goals never create urgency; deadlines with witnesses do.
Why it works
  • Deadline proximity reliably increases effort allocation.
  • A single metric prevents the effort dilution that kills multi-goal quarters.
  • Public reporting converts private slippage into visible slippage.
How to run it

1Pick one metric

Something countable weekly: episodes shipped, clients called, kilometres run.

2Set the 100-day target

Ambitious but arithmetic — divide by weeks to get the weekly rate.

3Report weekly

Same day, same place, whether the number is good or bad.

13Henriette Anne Klauser: Write It Down, Make It Happen

From Write It Down, Make It Happen

Klauser's system is deceptively simple: the act of writing recruits attention and changes what you notice, turning a vague wish into an active filter on the world.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, with a pen and a page.
  • What: A written record of the goal, restated in your own handwriting, revisited often.
  • Where: A dedicated notebook — the friction of finding it is part of the ritual.
  • When: At the outset and again whenever the goal feels abstract.
  • Why: Attention is the scarce resource; writing allocates it.
Why it works
  • Handwriting engages deeper encoding than typing, improving recall.
  • Explicit goals prime perceptual filters to detect relevant opportunities.
  • Re-reading written goals repeatedly re-activates that priming.
How to run it

1Write the goal by hand

Present tense, dated, in a fixed notebook.

2Log evidence

Note anything you notice during the week that relates to the goal.

3Re-read weekly

During the weekly review, before you plan the next week.

14BJ Fogg: B = MAP and Tiny Habits

From Tiny Habits

Fogg's model states behaviour occurs when Motivation, Ability and a Prompt converge. Since motivation fluctuates, a reliable system maximises ability and engineers the prompt.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, and the environment supplying the prompt.
  • What: A behaviour shrunk until it can be done on your worst day, anchored to an existing routine.
  • Where: Immediately after an existing habit in the same physical location.
  • When: Every time the anchor fires.
  • Why: Motivation is unreliable; ability and prompts are designable.
Why it works
  • Behaviour requires all three factors simultaneously — removing any one prevents it.
  • Celebration immediately after the behaviour wires in positive emotion, which drives repetition.
  • Shrinking scope raises ability far faster than motivation techniques raise motivation.
How to run it

1Write the recipe

'After I [anchor], I will [tiny behaviour].'

2Shrink to trivial

Floss one tooth; two push-ups; open the document.

3Celebrate immediately

A genuine three-second 'yes!' right after — this is the wiring step.

15Cal Newport: Deep Work Scheduling

From Deep Work

Newport's system treats undistracted concentration as a trainable capacity with a daily ceiling, then protects it with rituals, shutdowns and scheduled shallow work.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, with colleagues informed of the ritual.
  • What: Fixed daily deep blocks, a shutdown ritual, and batched shallow work.
  • Where: A single dedicated location associated only with deep work.
  • When: Same hours daily; typically 90–240 minutes, never more than four.
  • Why: Depth is rare, valuable and disappearing — which makes it leverage.
Why it works
  • Attention residue from switching degrades performance for tens of minutes.
  • Deep work capacity is finite per day and trainable over months.
  • A shutdown ritual closes open loops, which is what actually enables recovery.
How to run it

1Choose a depth philosophy

Rhythmic daily blocks suit most people with normal jobs.

2Ritualise entry

Same place, same start time, same first action, phone in another room.

3Shut down completely

A scripted end-of-day review and a spoken phrase that ends work.

16Carol Dweck: Growth-Mindset Feedback Loops

From Mindset

Dweck's contribution to systems is interpretive: how you explain a bad week determines whether the system gets adjusted or abandoned.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, in the moment of interpreting a result.
  • What: A deliberate reframe applied to every failure the system produces.
  • Where: At the review step, written down rather than left as a feeling.
  • When: Immediately after any miss, and at the weekly review.
  • Why: Systems only improve if failures are treated as data.
Why it works
  • Attributing failure to effort and strategy sustains persistence; attributing it to ability ends it.
  • Process praise raises challenge-seeking; ability praise reduces it.
  • 'Not yet' language keeps the outcome in the future rather than closing it.
How to run it

1Rename the failure

Write 'this method didn't work yet' instead of 'I failed'.

2Change one variable

Adjust exactly one thing — time, place, size — and re-test for a week.

3Praise the process

Log effort, strategy and consistency in the tracker, not just outcomes.

17Nir Eyal: Indistractable Timeboxing

From Indistractable

Eyal's system starts from internal triggers: distraction is an escape from discomfort. The fix is a timeboxed schedule made in advance plus pacts that raise the cost of leaving it.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, plus the apps and people who interrupt you.
  • What: A calendar with no blank space, hacked-back external triggers, and effort/price/identity pacts.
  • Where: Everywhere — device settings, workspace layout and calendar.
  • When: Schedule weekly; handle internal triggers in the moment.
  • Why: You cannot call something a distraction unless you planned what it distracted you from.
Why it works
  • Discomfort, not technology, initiates most distraction episodes.
  • Surfing the urge — observing it for ten minutes — reliably dissolves it.
  • Pre-commitment devices work because they change the cost structure of quitting.
How to run it

1Timebox the whole week

Every hour gets a label, including rest and play.

2Hack back triggers

Turn off all non-human notifications; batch messages twice daily.

3Make a pact

Effort pact (site blocker), price pact (money at stake) or identity pact.

18Thibaut Meurisse: Master Your Emotions as System Maintenance

From Master Your Emotions / Success Bundle

Meurisse frames emotional state as a system input you can service: sleep, movement, information diet and self-talk determine whether the rest of the system runs.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, treating mood as maintenance rather than identity.
  • What: A short daily protocol that stabilises the physiological inputs to motivation.
  • Where: Morning and evening, at home.
  • When: Daily, with a weekly audit of which input slipped.
  • Why: Most 'motivation problems' are sleep, movement or input problems.
Why it works
  • Emotions follow physiology with a lag — sleep debt shows up as apathy days later.
  • Naming an emotion reduces amygdala activation and restores executive control.
  • Information diet shapes baseline arousal more than most people expect.
How to run it

1Fix the wake time

One constant across all seven days; the rest of the rhythm follows it.

2Move before you decide

Ten minutes of movement before any demanding decision.

3Run a written reframe

Name the emotion, name the trigger, name the next action.

19Grant Cardone: The 10X Input System

From The 10X Rule

Cardone's system multiplies inputs rather than refining targets: estimate the required action, multiply by ten, and let volume solve the accuracy problem.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, when you've been consistently underestimating.
  • What: A daily activity quota set an order of magnitude above the comfortable estimate.
  • Where: Wherever output is produced — calls, reps, drafts, shipments.
  • When: Daily, counted, non-negotiable.
  • Why: Most goals fail from under-action, not from bad strategy.
Why it works
  • Planning fallacy causes systematic underestimation of time and effort.
  • High volume produces more feedback cycles, which accelerates skill.
  • Massive action reframes rejection as statistical noise rather than personal failure.
How to run it

1Estimate, then multiply

Whatever you think it takes, set the quota at ten times.

2Count the inputs

Track the activity, not the outcome — inputs are the controllable part.

3Never lower the quota

Adjust the method, not the volume.

20David Allen: Getting Things Done

From Getting Things Done

GTD is the canonical personal system: capture everything, clarify what it means, organise by context, reflect weekly, and engage from trusted lists.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, plus every inbox in your life.
  • What: A closed-loop system of lists: next actions, projects, waiting-for, someday/maybe.
  • Where: One capture tool always with you; contexts defined by tool and place.
  • When: Capture continuously, clarify daily, reflect weekly.
  • Why: Open loops consume attention whether or not you're working on them.
Why it works
  • The Zeigarnik effect keeps unfinished tasks intrusive until they're recorded in a trusted system.
  • Trust is the operative variable — an unreviewed list stops being relieving.
  • Deciding the very next physical action removes the ambiguity that causes procrastination.
How to run it

1Do a mind sweep

Empty everything on your mind into a single inbox — expect 100+ items.

2Define next actions

Each item becomes a concrete physical action or is filed/deleted.

3Hold the weekly review

Non-negotiable; without it the system quietly becomes untrusted.

21Jim Rohn: The Daily Disciplines Compound

From The Art of Exceptional Living / 7 Strategies

Rohn's system is philosophical arithmetic: success is a few simple disciplines practised daily, and failure is a few errors in judgement repeated daily. The difference only becomes visible over years.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, doing ordinary things with unreasonable consistency.
  • What: A short list of daily disciplines — reading, planning, health, and a written journal.
  • Where: In ordinary life, not in special circumstances.
  • When: Daily, for years; the payoff is back-loaded.
  • Why: "Success is nothing more than a few simple disciplines practised every day."
Why it works
  • Compounding is invisible early, which is precisely why most people quit before it shows.
  • Working harder on yourself than on your job changes your earning capacity, not just output.
  • The philosophy that governs your choices produces the results — change the philosophy first.
How to run it

1Choose four disciplines

Read 30 minutes, plan the day, move the body, review the numbers.

2Keep a journal

Rohn's own record: what you learned, what you'd change, what you noticed.

3Measure yearly, not weekly

Judge the system on twelve-month evidence, not on a bad fortnight.

22Zig Ziglar: The Wheel of Life Balance System

From See You at the Top / Goals

Ziglar's system spans seven life areas and requires each goal to pass a checklist — because a system that optimises one domain while wrecking the others isn't success.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, auditing all seven areas rather than one.
  • What: A goals programme: written goal, benefit list, obstacles, skills needed, people needed, plan, date.
  • Where: In a written goals book, reviewed regularly.
  • When: Annual set, weekly review, daily action.
  • Why: Lopsided achievement eventually collapses the areas it ignored.
Why it works
  • Explicit benefit-listing raises commitment by making the payoff concrete.
  • Pre-listing obstacles is a rehearsal that reduces surprise-driven abandonment.
  • Balance across domains protects the energy the ambitious domain depends on.
How to run it

1Score all seven areas

Rate each 1–10 today; the lowest two get attention first.

2Complete the goal checklist

Benefits, obstacles, skills, people, plan, deadline — for each goal.

3Review weekly

Read the goals book at the same time as your weekly review.

23Tony Robbins: RPM: Results, Purpose, Massive Action

From Awaken the Giant Within

Robbins replaces to-do lists with an outcome-focused planning system: name the result, name the purpose, then generate a massive action plan and prioritise it.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, at the weekly planning session.
  • What: An RPM block per major outcome, with purpose written before actions.
  • Where: In a planning document reviewed daily.
  • When: Weekly for the plan; daily for the priority list.
  • Why: Purpose supplies the energy that makes the action plan survive contact with reality.
Why it works
  • Outcome framing reduces busywork by making every action justify itself.
  • Stated purpose ('why') sustains effort when the action list becomes unpleasant.
  • State management — physiology, focus, language — is a controllable input to execution.
How to run it

1Brain-dump and chunk

List everything, then group items under the outcome they serve.

2Write result and purpose

One sentence each, purpose in emotional language.

3Build the MAP

List every possible action, then mark the few that are must-do.

24Peter Drucker: Management by Objectives and Self-Control

From The Effective Executive

Drucker's system applies management discipline to yourself: know where your time actually goes, focus on contribution, build on strengths, and make decisions once.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, as the manager of your own knowledge work.
  • What: A recorded time log, a contribution statement, and feedback analysis on decisions.
  • Where: In your calendar and a decision journal.
  • When: Log time for two weeks each quarter; review decisions after 6–12 months.
  • Why: "What gets measured gets managed" applies first to your own hours.
Why it works
  • Memory of time use is systematically wrong; only a contemporaneous log is accurate.
  • Feedback analysis — writing predicted outcomes and comparing later — reveals real strengths.
  • Effectiveness is a habit set, not a talent.
How to run it

1Log your time

Record actual usage in 30-minute blocks for two weeks; then prune.

2Write a contribution statement

What results does this role owe, and to whom?

3Keep a decision journal

Record the decision, the expectation and the date to review it.

25Edwin Locke & Gary Latham: Goal-Setting Theory

From A Theory of Goal Setting & Task Performance

The research backbone under every other framework here: specific, difficult goals produce higher performance than vague ones, mediated by direction, effort, persistence and strategy.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: Anyone setting a performance target for themselves or a team.
  • What: Specific, difficult, committed goals with feedback and task-relevant strategy.
  • Where: Any performance context — the effect is one of the most replicated in psychology.
  • When: At target-setting time; feedback must be continuous.
  • Why: 'Do your best' produces measurably worse results than a hard number.
Why it works
  • Four mediators: direction of attention, effort mobilisation, persistence and strategy development.
  • Feedback is a necessary moderator — a hard goal without feedback loses its effect.
  • For novel complex tasks, learning goals beat outcome goals until competence exists.
How to run it

1Make it specific and hard

Replace 'get fitter' with a number and a date.

2Secure commitment

Importance plus self-efficacy; without both, difficulty backfires.

3Instrument the feedback

Track the number weekly so the goal keeps steering behaviour.

26Gabriele Oettingen: WOOP / Mental Contrasting

From Rethinking Positive Thinking

Oettingen shows fantasising about success depletes energy. WOOP pairs the wish and outcome with the real obstacle and a pre-set plan, converting daydreams into commitment.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, in five minutes, without any tools.
  • What: A four-step mental exercise that ends with an if-then plan.
  • Where: Anywhere quiet; it's entirely internal.
  • When: Daily for ongoing goals; before any difficult task.
  • Why: Positive fantasy alone predicts lower achievement — contrast is what makes it work.
Why it works
  • Mental contrasting creates a non-conscious association between obstacle and action.
  • Indulging in success imagery lowers physiological arousal, reducing effort.
  • The obstacle must be internal — the real blocker is rarely external.
How to run it

1Name the wish

One challenging, feasible wish for the next four weeks.

2Imagine the outcome, then the obstacle

Twenty seconds each, vividly, in that order.

3Set the if-then

'If [obstacle occurs], then I will [specific action].'

27Peter Gollwitzer: Implementation Intentions

From Implementation Intentions research

Gollwitzer's finding is the highest-leverage single technique in behaviour change: pre-deciding when, where and how doubles to triples follow-through.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, at planning time rather than action time.
  • What: An if-then plan specifying situational cue and behavioural response.
  • Where: Written where you'll see it before the cue occurs.
  • When: Set in advance; the plan runs automatically at the cue.
  • Why: It delegates control of the behaviour from intention to the environment.
Why it works
  • The plan creates a strong cue-response link retrieved automatically when the cue appears.
  • Effects are largest exactly where willpower is weakest — fatigue, stress, temptation.
  • Coping plans for anticipated obstacles outperform generic motivation.
How to run it

1Specify the cue precisely

Time, place and preceding event — not 'when I have time'.

2Specify the response

One concrete action, not a category of actions.

3Write both down

'If it's 7am and I'm in the kitchen, then I put my running shoes on.'

28Angela Duckworth: Grit and Deliberate-Practice Systems

From Grit

Duckworth's system is hierarchical: one top-level goal, mid-level goals that serve it, and low-level tasks that are all replaceable. Grit is holding the top level constant while swapping the rest.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, over a horizon of years.
  • What: A written goal hierarchy plus a daily deliberate-practice slot.
  • Where: In a document you revisit each quarter.
  • When: Daily practice; quarterly hierarchy review.
  • Why: Consistency of direction over years explains achievement better than talent.
Why it works
  • Deliberate practice requires a stretch target, full focus, immediate feedback and repetition.
  • Interest deepens with competence — passion is usually developed, not discovered.
  • Hope, defined as the belief effort improves the future, sustains effort after setbacks.
How to run it

1Draw the hierarchy

One top goal; cross out any mid-goal that doesn't serve it.

2Book the practice slot

Same time daily, on the weakest sub-skill, with feedback.

3Change tactics, not the summit

Swap low-level tasks freely; keep the top level fixed.

29Charles Duhigg: The Habit Loop and Keystone Habits

From The Power of Habit

Duhigg's system diagnoses an existing habit rather than adding a new one: keep the cue and reward, change only the routine — and prioritise keystone habits that cascade.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, plus a group when the habit is stubborn.
  • What: A diagnostic experiment on one existing loop, then a substituted routine.
  • Where: At the place the cue reliably occurs.
  • When: Over three to four weeks of testing.
  • Why: You can't extinguish a loop — you can only replace the routine inside it.
Why it works
  • Cues fall into five categories: location, time, emotional state, other people, preceding action.
  • Belief, often supplied by a community, is what makes changed loops survive stress.
  • Keystone habits (exercise, family dinner, making the bed) reorganise unrelated behaviours.
How to run it

1Log the five cue categories

For a week, record all five whenever the habit fires.

2Test different rewards

Swap the reward and note whether the craving is satisfied.

3Write the new plan

'When [cue], I will [new routine] because it provides [reward].'

30Wendy Wood: Habit Science: Friction and Context

From Good Habits, Bad Habits

Wood's research shows roughly 43% of daily behaviour is habitual. Her system therefore works on context and friction rather than on goals or willpower.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, changing the space rather than the self.
  • What: Systematic reduction of friction for good behaviours and addition for bad ones.
  • Where: In the physical and digital environments where behaviour happens.
  • When: Once, at design time — then it works passively.
  • Why: Habits persist because context cues them, not because you decided to.
Why it works
  • Habits are context-cue driven and largely insensitive to current goals or intentions.
  • Even 20 seconds of added friction meaningfully suppresses a behaviour.
  • Disruptions — moving house, new job — are windows where habits can be rewritten.
How to run it

1Do a friction audit

For each target behaviour, count the steps required and cut them.

2Add 20-second barriers

Log out, unplug, store it in the garage, delete the app.

3Use disruption windows

Install new habits during moves, role changes and holidays.

31Katy Milkman: Temptation Bundling and Fresh Starts

From How to Change

Milkman's system matches a tactic to the specific obstacle: forgetting, laziness, impulsivity, confidence — each has a different fix, and fresh-start dates make change easier to launch.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, diagnosing which obstacle you actually have.
  • What: A tactic chosen to match the obstacle, launched on a fresh-start date.
  • Where: Wherever the obstacle bites.
  • When: Launch on a Monday, a first-of-month or a birthday for the fresh-start effect.
  • Why: Generic advice fails because it treats different obstacles identically.
Why it works
  • The fresh-start effect: temporal landmarks increase aspirational behaviour.
  • Temptation bundling makes the want-to activity only available during the should-do one.
  • Commitment devices work by removing future options from your own control.
How to run it

1Diagnose the obstacle

Be honest: is it forgetting, impulsivity, laziness or low confidence?

2Bundle a temptation

Audiobooks or a show only during the gym, only during the chore.

3Launch on a landmark

Start the new system on a date that already feels like a boundary.

32Albert Bandura: Self-Efficacy Engineering

From Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control

Bandura shows belief in your capability predicts persistence better than actual skill — and self-efficacy is buildable from four specific sources.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, and models who resemble you.
  • What: A deliberate ladder of small wins plus exposure to relevant models.
  • Where: In the domain where confidence is low.
  • When: Early — before difficulty rises.
  • Why: Efficacy determines how long you persist when the system gets hard.
Why it works
  • Mastery experiences are by far the strongest source — success must be experienced, not imagined.
  • Models are effective in proportion to how similar they seem to you.
  • Interpreting arousal as readiness rather than fear changes performance.
How to run it

1Build a win ladder

Sequence tasks from certain success to genuine stretch.

2Find a near-peer model

Someone one step ahead, not a distant expert.

3Reframe arousal

Label nerves as readiness; the physiology is identical.

33Roy Baumeister: Willpower Budgeting

From Willpower

Baumeister's practical claim: self-control is expensive and depletable in the short run, so a good system minimises how often it's needed.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, planning the shape of the day.
  • What: A schedule that places demanding decisions early and automates the rest.
  • Where: Across the whole daily schedule, including meals.
  • When: Design weekly; enforce daily.
  • Why: Every avoided decision is willpower conserved for the ones that matter.
Why it works
  • Decision-making and self-control draw on a shared, short-run limited resource.
  • Glucose, sleep and rest measurably restore self-control capacity.
  • Habits and pre-commitment bypass the resource entirely.
How to run it

1Front-load hard decisions

Anything requiring judgement goes before lunch.

2Automate the trivial

Standard meals, standard clothes, standard routes, standard start times.

3Guard sleep

Sleep debt is the fastest route to a collapsed system.

34Teresa Amabile: The Progress Principle

From The Progress Principle

Amabile's diary research found the single strongest driver of good inner work life is making progress in meaningful work — which makes visible small wins a system component, not a nicety.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, and anyone you lead.
  • What: A daily progress log plus removal of the 'inhibitors' that block small wins.
  • Where: At the end of each working day.
  • When: Daily, three minutes.
  • Why: Perceived progress, not reward, is the main engine of sustained motivation.
Why it works
  • Small wins have disproportionate effects on emotion, perception and drive.
  • Setbacks hurt roughly two to three times more than equivalent wins help.
  • Catalysts (clear goals, resources, autonomy) and nourishers (respect, encouragement) enable progress.
How to run it

1Keep a progress diary

One line each evening: what moved forward today.

2Remove one inhibitor weekly

Unclear goals, missing tools, needless approvals.

3Make progress visible

Charts and streaks in this app exist for exactly this reason.

35Stephen Guise: Mini Habits

From Mini Habits

Guise's system sets targets so small they're 'stupid small' — one push-up, fifty words — because the binding constraint is starting, and small targets never trigger resistance.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, when consistency keeps collapsing.
  • What: A daily requirement small enough that failure is essentially impossible.
  • Where: Anywhere; the target must be doable in bad conditions.
  • When: Every single day — the non-negotiability is the mechanism.
  • Why: A tiny requirement plus unlimited overshoot beats a big requirement plus frequent failure.
Why it works
  • Small targets bypass the brain's resistance to effort, so initiation costs almost nothing.
  • Overshoot is common and unmeasured — the requirement is a floor, not a ceiling.
  • Uninterrupted streaks build identity evidence faster than sporadic large efforts.
How to run it

1Halve it, then halve again

Until the requirement feels almost embarrassing.

2Never raise the requirement

Raise the average by overshooting, not by raising the floor.

3Track the floor only

Credit the day when the minimum is met, regardless of extras.

36Darren Hardy: The Compound Effect

From The Compound Effect

Hardy's system is measurement-first: track the small choices in one area for a month, because tracking alone changes behaviour and reveals where the compounding is leaking.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, in exactly one area at a time.
  • What: A written tracker of every relevant choice for 30 days, then correction.
  • Where: Carried with you — the tracking must be immediate, not reconstructed.
  • When: Daily for a month per area.
  • Why: You cannot manage what you refuse to look at.
Why it works
  • Self-monitoring alone produces measurable behaviour change (the reactivity effect).
  • Momentum ('Big Mo') takes weeks of consistency to appear and moments of inconsistency to lose.
  • Small differences are invisible short-term and decisive long-term.
How to run it

1Pick one area

Money, food, time or training — one only, for 30 days.

2Track every instance

Every purchase, every bite, every hour, written at the moment.

3Cut the worst input

At day 30, remove the single largest leak and re-run.

37Jocko Willink: Discipline Equals Freedom / Extreme Ownership

From Discipline Equals Freedom

Willink's system removes negotiation from the day: fixed wake time, default action, and total ownership of every failure — which makes the fix always something you control.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, without exceptions or negotiations.
  • What: Fixed standards — wake time, training, preparation — treated as non-optional.
  • Where: Everywhere; the point is that conditions don't alter the standard.
  • When: Daily, starting before dawn in Willink's own practice.
  • Why: Discipline produces freedom because it removes the daily argument.
Why it works
  • Removing the decision removes the fatigue and the negotiation that precedes failure.
  • Ownership language directs attention at controllable variables, which is where fixes live.
  • Default aggression — 'when in doubt, go' — beats deliberation for small daily choices.
How to run it

1Fix the wake time

Same alarm every day, including weekends. Get up on the first ring.

2Prepare the night before

Kit laid out; the morning contains no decisions.

3Own every miss

Write the controllable cause and the process change, not the excuse.

38Robin Sharma: The 5AM Club 20/20/20 Formula

From The 5AM Club

Sharma's system claims the first hour: twenty minutes moving, twenty reflecting, twenty growing — a fixed structure that guarantees the day's most valuable inputs occur.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, before the household or the inbox wakes.
  • What: A 60-minute structured first hour, plus a matching evening shutdown.
  • Where: A prepared space; no devices allowed inside the hour.
  • When: 05:00–06:00, daily, with the phone left outside the room.
  • Why: The first hour sets the quality of every hour after it.
Why it works
  • Early rising works only when paired with a protected earlier bedtime.
  • Intense movement early raises alertness and mood for hours.
  • Habit installation takes roughly 66 days on average — expect a hard first month.
How to run it

1Shift bedtime first

Move sleep earlier for two weeks before moving the alarm.

2Run 20/20/20 exactly

Sweat, then journal/plan, then read or study — same order daily.

3Add an evening shutdown

Devices off 60 minutes before bed; the morning is won at night.

39Tim Ferriss: DiSSS Meta-Learning and the 80/20 Audit

From The 4-Hour Workweek / The 4-Hour Chef

Ferriss builds systems for learning and elimination: deconstruct a skill to its minimal effective units, then eliminate, automate and delegate everything else.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, plus tools and people to whom work can be shifted.
  • What: A minimal effective dose of practice, with everything else eliminated or automated.
  • Where: In the skill domain and across your whole task inventory.
  • When: Audit quarterly; practise daily under real stakes.
  • Why: Most effort is spent on activities that produce almost none of the results.
Why it works
  • Pareto distributions appear reliably across tasks, customers and time use.
  • Minimum effective dose: more input past the threshold produces no additional result.
  • Real stakes — money or reputation — accelerate learning far more than good intentions.
How to run it

1Run an 80/20 audit

List activities and results; cut the bottom 80% of activities ruthlessly.

2Deconstruct the skill

Find the few units that produce most of the capability.

3Add stakes

Book the exam, the race or the demo before you feel ready.

40Chris McChesney: The 4 Disciplines of Execution

From The 4 Disciplines of Execution

4DX is the most rigorous execution system here: focus on a wildly important goal, act on lead measures, keep a compelling scoreboard and hold a weekly cadence of accountability.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, or a small team of two to eight.
  • What: One WIG, two or three lead measures, a visible scoreboard and a 20-minute weekly meeting.
  • Where: The scoreboard must be physically or digitally visible, not filed away.
  • When: Weekly WIG session, same day, same time, no exceptions.
  • Why: The whirlwind of daily urgency defeats every strategy that isn't defended weekly.
Why it works
  • Lead measures are predictive and influenceable; lag measures are neither.
  • A scoreboard players understand at a glance changes behaviour; a manager's dashboard doesn't.
  • Peer commitment in a weekly cadence is what converts intention into execution.
How to run it

1Name one WIG

From X to Y by when. One only — focus is the whole point.

2Choose lead measures

Weekly behaviours you fully control that predict the WIG.

3Run the weekly cadence

Report last week's commitment, review the board, commit for next week.

41John Doerr: OKRs — Objectives and Key Results

From Measure What Matters

Doerr's system separates the qualitative direction (Objective) from three to five measurable outcomes (Key Results), scored transparently each quarter.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, with everything visible to whoever holds you accountable.
  • What: Quarterly objectives with 3–5 numeric key results, scored 0.0–1.0.
  • Where: In a shared document — transparency is a core feature of the system.
  • When: Set quarterly, checked weekly, scored at quarter end.
  • Why: Stretch OKRs scoring 0.7 are healthy; consistent 1.0 means the targets were too soft.
Why it works
  • Separating direction from measurement stops goals from becoming unfalsifiable.
  • Transparency creates alignment and social accountability simultaneously.
  • Scoring, rather than pass/fail, preserves information about near-misses.
How to run it

1Write the objective

Qualitative, inspirational, time-bound — no numbers here.

2Add 3–5 key results

Each numeric with a baseline and a target.

3Score honestly

0.7 on stretch goals is a good quarter; grade and reset.

42Simon Sinek: Start With Why as System Foundation

From Start With Why / The Infinite Game

Sinek's contribution is durability: a system anchored to a stated cause survives setbacks that a system anchored to a target does not, because the cause has no completion date.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, defining the cause before the routine.
  • What: A written 'why' statement that every habit in the system must serve.
  • Where: At the top of your planning document.
  • When: Written once, revisited annually.
  • Why: Finite goals end; a just cause keeps the system running past them.
Why it works
  • Purpose statements engage the limbic system, which drives behaviour and decision-making.
  • An infinite mindset reframes setbacks as position changes, not defeats.
  • Consistency, not intensity, is what builds trust — in others and in yourself.
How to run it

1Write the why

'To ___ so that ___.' One sentence, no metrics.

2Test each habit

If a habit doesn't serve the why, cut it or change the why.

3Name a worthy rival

Someone whose strengths reveal what your system lacks.

43Daniel Pink: Autonomy, Mastery, Purpose

From Drive

Pink's system designs for intrinsic motivation: give the routine real autonomy, a visible mastery curve and an explicit purpose, and external pressure becomes unnecessary.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, designing your own conditions.
  • What: Task, time, technique and team choices retained by you, aimed at a purpose.
  • Where: In how the work itself is structured.
  • When: Reviewed whenever the system starts feeling like an obligation.
  • Why: Contingent rewards degrade intrinsic motivation for anything beyond routine tasks.
Why it works
  • The overjustification effect: paying for an enjoyable behaviour reduces its intrinsic appeal.
  • Mastery is asymptotic — the pull comes from approach, not arrival.
  • Purpose maximisation sustains effort where profit maximisation stalls.
How to run it

1Reclaim one of the four Ts

Choose your task, time, technique or team on at least one project.

2Make mastery visible

Track a skill curve, not just completion ticks.

3State the purpose

Write who benefits when the system runs well.

44Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi: Designing for Flow

From Flow

Csikszentmihalyi's system tunes the difficulty of daily work so that challenge slightly exceeds skill — the band where attention becomes effortless and the system runs itself.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, adjusting the difficulty dial daily.
  • What: Clear goals, immediate feedback and challenge calibrated just above current skill.
  • Where: In the task itself, and in the environment that protects it.
  • When: In blocks of 60–120 minutes without interruption.
  • Why: Flow is both the most productive and the most enjoyable state — it is designable.
Why it works
  • Flow requires clear proximal goals and immediate feedback, or attention fragments.
  • Anxiety signals challenge is too high; boredom signals skill has outgrown the task.
  • Autotelic experience makes the behaviour self-sustaining — no external reward needed.
How to run it

1Set a proximal goal

Define what 'done well' means for this session, before starting.

2Build in feedback

A metric visible during the work, not after it.

3Tune the difficulty

Bored? Add a constraint. Anxious? Shrink the scope.

45Greg McKeown: Essentialism and Effortless Design

From Essentialism / Effortless

McKeown's system is disciplined subtraction: fewer commitments, chosen deliberately, then made as effortless as possible to execute repeatedly.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, protecting your own agenda from other people's.
  • What: A 90% rule for commitments plus effortless design of the remaining few.
  • Where: At the point of every incoming request.
  • When: Every time you're asked for time; formally at quarterly review.
  • Why: If it isn't a clear yes, it's a no — undecided commitments accumulate silently.
Why it works
  • Decision fatigue and the sunk-cost effect make removal harder than addition.
  • Explicit criteria make saying no a policy rather than a confrontation.
  • Designing the easiest first step converts intention into action reliably.
How to run it

1Apply the 90% rule

Score each opportunity 0–100; below 90 is a no.

2Define your essential intent

One sentence, concrete and inspirational, for the year.

3Make the right thing effortless

Cut steps until the essential action is the path of least resistance.

46Ryan Holiday: Stoic Operating Principles

From The Obstacle Is the Way / The Daily Stoic

Holiday's system supplies the mental discipline layer: the dichotomy of control decides where effort is spent, and a daily journal keeps the system honest.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, first thing in the morning and last thing at night.
  • What: A morning intention and evening review, filtered through what you actually control.
  • Where: In a journal kept for that purpose only.
  • When: Twice daily, five minutes each.
  • Why: Wasting effort on the uncontrollable is the most common systems leak.
Why it works
  • Premeditatio malorum — rehearsing setbacks — reduces their disruptive force.
  • Voluntary discomfort widens the range of conditions in which the system still runs.
  • Journalling externalises reasoning and makes self-deception visible.
How to run it

1Sort the day

Two columns each morning: controllable and not. Work only the first.

2Rehearse the obstacle

Name what could go wrong and your pre-decided response.

3Review at night

What did I do well, badly, and differently tomorrow?

47Benjamin Hardy: Willpower Doesn't Work — Design the Environment

From Willpower Doesn't Work / Personality Isn't Permanent

Hardy's system argues willpower is evidence of poor design. Change the situation — forcing functions, peer group, physical space — and behaviour follows without struggle.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, plus the people you spend the most time with.
  • What: Deliberate redesign of physical, social and systemic environments around the goal.
  • Where: In all three layers simultaneously — one alone rarely holds.
  • When: At the start, and again whenever you notice yourself relying on willpower.
  • Why: If you need willpower daily, the environment is misconfigured.
Why it works
  • Situations shape behaviour more powerfully than personality traits do.
  • Forcing functions create unavoidable consequences that make the behaviour inevitable.
  • Peer groups reset the perceived normal, which resets the baseline standard.
How to run it

1Create a forcing function

Pay in advance, publish the date, sign the contract.

2Upgrade the peer group

Spend regular time with people whose normal is your stretch.

3Build a single-purpose space

One location used only for the behaviour you want automated.

48Marshall Goldsmith: Daily Questions and Active Accountability

From Triggers

Goldsmith's system is a nightly self-scored questionnaire: 'Did I do my best to…' — phrasing that measures effort rather than outcome, with a coach or partner reading the score.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, plus one person who hears the scores.
  • What: Six to twelve 'Did I do my best to…' questions scored 1–10 every night.
  • Where: A spreadsheet or tracker, reported to your partner.
  • When: Every night, without exception; reported weekly.
  • Why: Effort-framed questions restore agency; outcome questions invite excuses.
Why it works
  • 'Did I do my best to…' forces an internal attribution and removes external blame.
  • Daily self-scoring makes drift visible within days rather than months.
  • An external reader eliminates the quiet renegotiation that kills solo systems.
How to run it

1Write the questions

Cover health, relationships, work and learning; all effort-framed.

2Score every night

1–10, honestly, in under two minutes.

3Report to someone

A weekly message with the scores — no commentary needed.

49Dan Sullivan: The Gap and the Gain / Who Not How

From The Gap and the Gain

Sullivan's system fixes how progress is measured: measure backwards against where you started (the gain), not forwards against an ideal (the gap) — and solve bottlenecks with 'who', not 'how'.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, and the people who can do what you shouldn't.
  • What: Backwards measurement at every review, plus a 'who' for every recurring bottleneck.
  • Where: In the review step of your weekly and quarterly cadence.
  • When: Weekly gain review; quarterly 'who' audit.
  • Why: Ideals are useful as direction and toxic as a measuring stick.
Why it works
  • Measuring against an unreachable ideal guarantees a permanent deficit and eventual burnout.
  • Backwards measurement supplies the evidence that sustains self-efficacy.
  • Asking 'who can do this?' removes the capacity ceiling that 'how do I do this?' imposes.
How to run it

1List three gains weekly

Concrete evidence of progress since a fixed earlier date.

2Stop measuring against the ideal

Keep the ideal as direction only, never as a score.

3Find a who

For each recurring bottleneck, name a person, tool or service instead.

50Ray Dalio: Principles and the Five-Step Process

From Principles

Dalio's system is explicitly algorithmic: write down your principles, run a five-step loop on every goal, and treat pain plus reflection as the input that upgrades the machine.

The 5 Ws Blueprint
  • Who: You, operating on yourself as a machine you can redesign.
  • What: Written principles, an issue log, and a documented five-step loop per goal.
  • Where: In a principles document and a decision/issue log.
  • When: Continuously; formal diagnosis whenever a result misses.
  • Why: The machine that produces results can itself be inspected and improved.
Why it works
  • Root-cause diagnosis distinguishes proximate causes from the design flaw producing them.
  • Believability-weighted input beats both consensus and pure autonomy.
  • Recording principles turns one-off lessons into reusable decision rules.
How to run it

1Write your principles

Start with ten decision rules you already follow implicitly.

2Keep an issue log

Record every problem without softening it; no diagnosis without data.

3Run the five steps

Goal, problems, root cause, redesign, execute — in that order, every time.

⏳ Time Management Tools

A full toolkit for deciding what to do, when to do it, and how to protect the time once it's scheduled — drawn from the most-cited frameworks in the field.

🎯 Daily Highlight

From Make Time (Knapp & Zeratsky): before the day starts, name the one thing that would make today satisfying if nothing else got done — then protect time for it.

🚦 Eat That Frog

Brian Tracy's rule: identify your hardest, most consequential task and do it first, before anything else gets a chance to distract you.

⏳ 2-Minute Rule Inbox

From Getting Things Done: if a task takes under two minutes, do it immediately instead of letting it clog your list. Capture quick tasks here and check them off as you clear them.

🚫 Not-To-Do List

A reverse to-do list — recurring time-wasters, bad habits, or low-value requests you've decided to say no to on sight. Reviewing it before you plan your day prevents old leaks from reopening.

📋 Time Audit Log

Laura Vanderkam's core exercise from 168 Hours: log what you actually did with blocks of time, honestly, for a few days. Most people are surprised by where the hours really go — the log is the whole intervention.

Today's Log
By Category
💰 Weekly Time Budget

Elizabeth Grace Saunders' metaphor from How to Invest Your Time Like Money: budget your 168 hours a week across categories the way you'd budget a paycheck, so overspending in one area is a visible, deliberate trade-off rather than an accident.

📅 Timeboxing Template Library

Pick a ready-made daily structure and use it as a starting point. Timeboxing (distinct from the Time Blocking Planner above, which schedules your specific day) gives each type of work a maximum time limit up front, so tasks can't silently expand. Need to prioritize what goes in these boxes first? Use the Eisenhower Matrix in Planning.

📦 Task Batching Planner

Group similar low-context-switch tasks (calls, emails, errands) into a single batch instead of scattering them through the day — each context switch has a real, measurable refocus cost.

⚡ Energy-Level Scheduler

Daniel Pink's argument from When: most people have a predictable daily energy curve (peak, trough, recovery). Log how you actually feel at different hours, then match hard analytic work to your peak.

⌛ Deadline Compressor

Parkinson's Law: work expands to fill the time available for it. Give a task an artificially tight deadline and watch how much faster it actually gets done.

💧 Time Leak Self-Audit

A checklist of the most common, research-cited time leaks. Check any that apply to you honestly — the goal isn't guilt, it's visibility. Most people can name their biggest leak within the first five items.

🎓 Time Management Education

The core teachings behind the tools above — 50 of the most influential authors and books on managing time, attention, and priorities, from ancient Stoicism to modern productivity research. Each has its own diagram and, wherever possible, its own implementation tool.

Personal finance tools inspired by apps like YNAB, PocketGuard, and Rocket Money.

💰 Safe-to-Spend Daily Allowance

The PocketGuard idea: after bills, savings, and goal contributions are set aside, what's actually safe to spend today without derailing anything?

📂 Envelope Budgeting System

The Goodbudget method, digitized: give every dollar an envelope, spend from it, and stop when it hits zero.

🔁 Subscription Tracker

The Rocket Money idea: list every recurring subscription in one place — it's usually more than you think.

Small-business finance tools inspired by QuickBooks, Xero, and Float — for anyone running a side hustle or business alongside their personal budget.

🏆 Profit First Allocator

Mike Michalowicz's "Profit First" (2014): instead of Sales − Expenses = Profit, flip it — Sales − Profit = Expenses. Take your profit percentage off the top, first, every time revenue comes in.

⚖️ Break-Even Analysis (Business)

The classic small-business question: how many units (or how much revenue) do you need to cover your costs before you're making a profit?

🔮 Cash Flow Forecast (Business)

Click a quadrant below for a quick summary, or use the tabs for the full breakdown, transition roadmap, and a tool to map your own income.

🐙 GitHub Sync

Store your data file in a GitHub repository instead of (or as well as) this browser, so it follows you across devices and gets versioned automatically by git.

Read before using: use a private repository — anything in a public repo is world-readable, token or not. Your Personal Access Token is stored in this browser's local storage only (never committed), but it still grants write access to whatever it's scoped to, so use a fine-grained token limited to this one repo. This is data sync, not encryption — treat it accordingly.
